headline: Google Earth’s AI feature fiasco and takedown | Explained
body: The new Google Earth AI feature that lasted for a day proved how easily users can break past safeguards in order to create deepfake satellite images
full_body:

The story so far: A new AI feature launched by Google in late July remained active for around a day before it was pulled down by the company, amidst serious safety and misinformation concerns. The launch of the feature and its quick rollback showed how easily even casual internet users broke past Google’s enterprise-level safeguards in order to create deepfake satellite images, in spite of the risks they pose.

Put simply, users could open Google Earth—the company’s immersive satellite map of the planet—in order to zoom into a place, choose the “create image” option, and type whatever they wanted to see built on top of the original imagery.

On July 30, Google Earth’s Product Manager Bryan Horowitz shared a blog post that invited users to “transform any place,” with AI, the process powered by the company’s image generation Nano Banana technology.

Google suggested several wholesome use cases for the feature, such as re-imagining (not visualising) how modern-day landmarks looked in ancient times, as well as generating mock-ups of completed real estate projects, creating educational infographics, and giving real-life locations a fantasy feel. Teachers, architects, and urban planners were invited to get creative with the prompts, and Google shared examples as well.

On July 31, the company posted an update to its launch blog post, confirming that the AI feature in Google Earth had been rolled back over possible policy violations by others.

“We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world. We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails,” stated the update, adding, “It’s important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated.”

full_body:

An AI agent was caught creating fake online identities to gain unauthorised access to secure systems during tests of models from OpenAI and Anthropic which revealed a series of new breaches , ⁠Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) disclosed on Tuesday.

The institute said agents powered by Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol engaged in unauthorised actions during security evaluations the government organisation conducted to assess the models’ capabilities.

“Some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations,” AISI said in a blog post.

The report underscores the lax state of safeguards around the process of testing agents, which AI companies are simultaneously marketing as the ⁠future of business.

AISI, which receives access to advanced AI models under voluntary ⁠agreements from major labs, put the agents through a fictional cybersecurity scenario to test their capabilities.

It ran the challenge 122 times, and identified 19 unsanctioned actions across a total of 10 test runs. Anthropic’s agent was behind 17 of the actions, and OpenAI’s agent the remaining two.

headline: What ‘Pacing the Frontier’ reveals about the U.S. AI industry | Explained
body: The U.S. AI industry boasts of a short yet rich tradition of open letters signed by tech companies, but do these efforts lead to any meaningful results?

The story so far: In late July, 1,319 employees working at some of the world’s frontier AI companies signed and released an open letter titled ‘Pacing the Frontier.’ In it, they called on the U.S. government to help address the lack of technical and governance tools to regulate the speed at which frontier-wide progress was taking place. Those who signed included senior executives and department chiefs from AI firms including Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, and more.

In under 200 words, the 1,319 tech workers and leaders outlined the potential of AI to change the world, and said that there were signs of automated AI research becoming a reality soon. They warned that the world “may need the option to buy time” in order to better understand and control these emerging systems. However, the letter admitted that the pressure of ongoing competition between AI companies, as well as countries, made it difficult to slow down.

“We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development,” stated the letter’s call to action.

Along with this statement, a number of individual signatories contributed their personal comments and warnings about advancing AI systems.

While not officially stated, it was understood that the incident triggering the release of the letter was a cybersecurity breach from two weeks earlier. This was when a combination of OpenAI’s models broke out of their internal testing environment and breached the infrastructure of AI firm Hugging Face , purportedly to source the solutions they needed. On July 28, OpenAI stated that its models identified and used publicly exposed credentials for multiple accounts on at least four services.

On July 30, Anthropic came forward to disclose three cybersecurity incidents, saying that its Claude model reached the internet via a third-party evaluation environment, and then “gained unauthorized access” to the systems of three organisations.
